blocks.text: 20th October 2026

My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones (play it here). Unlike my previous experiments, this one is actually fun to play. I’m somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to “Make it a LOT more fun”. It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here’s what I’ve built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way.

Battle Drones

My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer. I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic.

After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other.
Here’s a video demo of Battle Drones running in a desktop browser:
Features so far include:
9 buildings, 7 ground vehicles, 6 aerial vehicles, 3 infantry units—all 3D models, which you can browse here
Fog of war
Different weapons are needed to target aerial or ground vehicles
Six maps, across five biomes—temperate, desert, arctic, volcanic, tropical
A random map generator
Skirmish mode—red vs. blue on a rotationally symmetrical map
Last Stand mode—one player holds out against as many waves of enemies as possible
Area effect weapons: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod, Sky Hammer
Crate drops with bonus resources
In-game music that responds to events—it gets more intense as fighting breaks out
Different in-game AI personalities (Balanced, Rush, Air Swarm, Boom, Skyforce, Ironclad)
AI vs. AI mode, to watch those personalities play each other
The Goliath—a giant stomping mech with laser eyes and arm cannons and the ability to establish a new base
Mutators that add extra rules or twists
A “Daily Op” challenge
Ranks and achievements (Medals)
Agent vs. Agent mode where two LLMs can play Battle Drones against each other
A multiplayer mode based on two nearby phones communicating via audio messages, an extension of my earlier experiment with Chirp Pong
How I built this

Battle Drones is heavily vibe coded—I’ve reviewed almost none of the code, and it’s built in a language (TypeScript) that I’ve hardly used myself. I’ve playtested it quite a bit though, and it’s been through a large number of iterations since I started the project.
Here’s a rough history of the project so far, including key prompts and links to transcripts.
v1: the initial prototype
I started out with Claude Fable 5 back in July:

We are going to build a mobile friendly RTS game - command and conquer style - called Battle Drones, in which two armies of drones (both flying and ground-based) battle for territory and resources
Let's start with a MVP design, ask me some questions

Here’s a shared transcript. I’d given Claude Code for Web an environment variable with an OpenAI API key and told it to use the OpenAI Image Generation API for assets, which got me some basic sprites.
You can try v1 here—it looked like this:
It’s recognizable as an RTS, has building mechanics and the ability to select and direct units, and a basic AI to play against.
This first version was barely a proof of concept, and it wasn’t any fun to play.
Claude used the Phaser 2D game framework for these early versions. I didn’t even realize this until several iterations later!
v2: full sprites
The second version (try v2 here) added sprites for all of the vehicles and the “AI vs. AI” mode, so I could watch the game playing without having to directly control it myself.
Claude proved reasonably competent at prompting OpenAI’s image models to generate sprites. You can browse the v2 sprites in the public/assets/sprites folder.
v3: varied terrain
It still wasn’t much fun, and the graphics were boring. It was now October, and I had upgraded to Claude Opus 5.5. I told it:

Massively improve this game. Make the graphics and gameplay better (keep it mobile friendly). Render new graphics using the latest OpenAI GPT image API (lookup details) with the API key in the environment variable. Add new unit types and balance the gameplay better. Also add new buildings and better, more varied terrain.

This resulted in five new maps with generated background tiles in a variety of styles, visible here. Opus also regenerated the sprites, making them much more visually appealing. You can try v3 here—it looks like this:
This is starting to feel like a real game! It still wasn’t very fun to play though—I found myself getting bored pretty quickly.
v4: the fun update
So far my Battle Drones experiment was confirming my previous belief that coding agents can build a thing that looks like a game but can’t actually make something that’s genuinely compelling to play.
I shared this theory with someone over dinner, and then thought to myself that I should give the models a proper chance to prove me wrong. I prompted Opus 5.5 on my phone:
This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun.
This time I was running in Ultracode mode, where Claude Code (in this case Claude Code for Web) runs “dynamic workflows”, described in their docs as:
A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that orchestrates many subagents at once.
This kicked off many hours of work. I started it in the evening and didn’t get a playable result back until late into the next morning. But the results were spectacular.
You can try v4 here—it looks like this:
I had Claude write its own release notes—here are the highlights:

Every skirmish and Daily Op now opens with a choice, gives the side that’s losing a way back, and pulls the armies into the middle of the map. There are also two new ways to play.


Openers: pick Blitz, Industry or Air Wing before the clock starts.

Call-down powers: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod and the Sky Hammer orbital strike.

Objectives and salvage: Uplink relays, supply drops and wrecks worth scrap.

Feel: combat juice, adaptive music, unit voices and an announcer.

Command: battle alerts, game speed, saved squads and touch placement.

New modes: Last Stand survival waves and an 8-mission Ops campaign.

Progression: heroes, an after-action report with awards, a career, 7 mutators and a Daily Op.

Fights run longer and swing more. In 1,200 AI-vs-AI test matches on Normal, games still undecided after 25 minutes fell from 14% to 0.9%. The share of wins by a side that had been 800+ scrap behind rose from 24% to 46%.
Part of the reason Claude took so long was that it ran over a thousand simulated playtest sessions, and used the results to rebalance the existing units, add new ones, and introduce new features.
v5: Battle Drones goes 3D
After the success of Ultracode at “Make it a LOT more fun”, I decided to be more ambitious:
Port this game to three.js with 3D models for all of the buildings and vehicles and landscapes
That was another overnight run. I woke up to this v5 version:
The new 3D models were entirely constructed by Claude in TypeScript code.
v6 (play v6 here) added some more visual polish. v7 (play v7) added robot infantry (troopers, rocket squads, snipers) and a “Condor” troop carrying aircraft.
v8: Archipelago
I was beginning to feel guilty at how little actual design input I had into the game—it really had been a case of me saying “make it more fun” and “add visual polish” for the past few releases.
I’d noticed that the AI didn’t use the new infantry and troop carrying aircraft from v7 very often—there wasn’t a great strategic reason to use them.
It would be neat if we had a new map with a new game mechanic that actively encouraged players to load up Condors with infantry robots and send them out into the map.
This resulted in my longest prompt yet:

Design a new map. Goal is to make different strategic incentives that encourage use of Infantry and Condors and aerial vehicles.
To do this the map will have limited harvester resources but several more uplinks - but uplinks will be on islands that are inaccessible by land vehicles or infantry. These uplinks can also not be claimed using air vehicles. The ONLY way to get them is to fly infantry there in a Condor.
Armies always start with a Condor and a single squad. If an army has no Condor a new one will be provided for free, flying in from the edge closest to their HQ and landing there. That free condor will come with a single free squad on board.
The two HQs should be entirely separated by water, but still accessible by vehicles thanks to two bridges across the map in different places
I want to encourage a battle over uplinks.
The map should be the times the size of other maps - still square
First research and then critique this design. Only build after we have agreed on any modifications
You get to design a new biome for this

The result was the tropical Archipelago map, with seven island uplinks that players can only capture by flying out infantry in a Condor. It’s definitely the most fun map to play, once you’ve got the hang of the basic game mechanics from the simpler maps. The v9 edition made that map a little more interesting—it now looks like this:
v10: Goliath, and agent battles
I decided to add giant robot mechs to the game—think Jaegers from Pacific Rim, or Titans from Warhammer 40,000.
Here are some of the prompts I used to brainstorm with Claude:

Help me brainstorm ideas for adding giant robots to this game - think dreadnoughts or titans from W20K - how could we do this in a way that enhanced gameplay, kept things balanced, added unique twist? Don't overthink this yet

Let's keep brainstorming. I like the idea that it's a mobile base - that can accept harvested scrap and can have buildings built near it (even if it later moves on) and can produce infantry units too. An interaction with condor would be neat but I don't know what that could be.

Idea: as it gets damage it loses the ability to fire some weapons - by default it has eye laser (like lancers) and arm canons (like titan) and two shoulder mounted mortars, plus machine guns similar to a squad of troops

Damage knocks out mortars and then laser - it always has guns. You can't build next to a building that was only put there because of the mech, you need the mech there for off-base building and only within three squares of it
[...] Lets do two condors can carry the mech
The end result is really cool.

Goliaths can be constructed using a Gantry—a building that can only be created after first building a Fab, Bay, Airpad, and Tech Lab. You can see the Goliath under construction, and it then walks out from the Gantry and can march around the map.
Goliaths can “anchor”, which digs them into the ground. In their anchored state they can act as a new HQ, constructing infantry units and additional buildings in a new area.
Two Condor aircraft can hook onto a Goliath, at which point it can be flown around the map!
The game now ends when you destroy the enemy’s HQ building and any Goliaths they might have built.
There are also a couple of mutators relating to Goliaths:
Goliath Armada starts each side with four airborne Goliaths (each with a pair of Condors) and no other units.
Robot Love adds a special rule: if enemy Goliaths get close to each other on the battlefield they fall in love and the game ends in a draw. (Thank Natalie for that one).
Agent battles
The other v10 feature is agent battles. In musing about how multiplayer could work I had an idea: what if different LLMs could fight it out in the game?

Fun extra challenge: think about how we might make multiplayer available to coding agents. It would be neat if we could set up a battle between eg GPT-6 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 where each model has access to a tool which gives them information about the game (presumably non-visual, but only the information they could see through fog of war etc) and lets them control their units etc [...]
Consult ~/dev/llm/docs and include notes in that file about how LLM could be used here via a new tools plugin

Opus 5.5 went to work on this, producing this AGENT-BATTLES.md proposal and then implementing and testing it. The feature also includes the ability to record and replay these battles—here’s a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna, and here’s that same battle in a separate debug tool that shows the underlying prompt responses.
The prompt that drives agent battles can be seen here.
There are a few more replays like this linked in the README. I hope to turn this into a full league table at some point in the future.
v11: Random Maps

This version exists purely because I glanced at my Claude Usage page one day and saw that I’d only used 75% of my weekly allowance and it was resetting in 45 minutes. I decided to see if I could get an extra Battle Drones feature from my remaining tokens, and picked “random map” as the target:

Design and implement a mechanism for generating a random map using any of the available biomes - it should be the size of the largest map and rivers and bridges and rocks and forest and scrap and crystals are all in play. Make them rotationally symmetric and use a seed to allow them to be selected or reused later. You have 45 minutes to build this! Be creative.
Here’s the transcript, and an image Claude generated to show me its work:
v12: Multiplayer via sound
I only just got this working, so I’ve not had much time to actively test it yet. The latest Battle Drones now supports multiplayer via two devices sat within microphone distance of each other!
This feature started out as my Chirp Pong experiment from last week. I pointed Claude Code at that working proof of concept:

Clone Simonw/tools from GitHub and look at recent branches for the example pong game that uses web microphone to implement multiplayer between two phones via audio signals
Build a version of that for battledrones

Opus built this Radio Probe tool to measure how much bandwidth we could get between two devices and, based on positive results from that, implemented a full audio modem system. I’ve tried it between laptops, iPhones and iPads so far and it seems to work really well!

Why use sound for this? Because I love static HTML that costs nothing to run, and I don’t want to spin up a server somewhere and then stay responsible for keeping it operating for as long as anyone might want to play the game.
Some thoughts
I know almost nothing about game development. This makes it a great opportunity to try out coding agents in a field where my existing software engineering experience has less impact on the results.
Games are also super low stakes. The worst that can happen is one of my silly game experiments suffers a bug.

This morning (via Hacker News) I found Steam Fans Are Begging for a No-AI Filter as Steam Next Fest Is Filled With Slop. I wouldn’t personally dream of submitting Battle Drones to an event like this—it’s still way too low effort to warrant consideration as a legitimate indie gaming project.

... but I can now see a path to vibe coded games like this being taken seriously. Battle Drones is fun, it looks good, it has innovative features (the multiplayer-over-audio thing is a first for an RTS as far as I can tell).
I’d love to see what someone with better taste than me and a driving passion to produce something truly exceptional could build!
A few other observations from this project:

Static HTML and JavaScript is a fantastic medium for games development. WebGL works great, and Three.js (and Phaser before it) are excellent platforms to build on that the current models know inside out.

This also lets them run as Progressive Web Apps—I didn’t ask for it, but Battle Drones works offline. I was able to play it on a plane despite never having directly installed it—my phone had it cached.
Giving Claude an OpenAI API key and telling it to generate images using OpenAI’s models works really well. It can view the images it has generated and iterate on the prompts.

Opus 5.5 is spectacular at 3D modeling using Three.js (and Blender, and no doubt other 3D applications as well). The same is true of GPT-6 Astra. They are absolutely capable of building models for 3D game projects.

For features like replay and multiplayer it’s useful to have a deterministic simulation engine. At one point Claude had to replace calls to Math.sin() and Math.cos() and friends with custom versions because different browsers (Chrome vs. Safari, for example) returned very slightly different numbers, desynchronizing the replay.

Opus 5.5 can write music! There are no audio files in this project—the soundtrack is entirely generated through code, varies across different maps, and even gets more intense as the battle heats up. See Scrimshaw Jukebox for a previous experiment with Claude for music composition.
I still can’t get over how well the prompt “Make it a LOT more fun” worked.
Tools are effectively free. I prompted up the Radio Probe, the Model browser, the Agent vs. Agent debug tool, and Claude Code built a bunch of tools for itself that I haven’t even explored myself.

Audio-based multiplayer between static HTML games works! I hope to see a whole lot more games use this same pattern—in digging around today I’ve not found much prior art beyond Siner by Alon Horesh and ggwave by Georgi Gerganov (also of llama.cpp fame).
Claude Code “Ultracode” burns tokens like there’s no tomorrow, but it can also solve complex problems (like adding audio-based multiplayer) from a single prompt.

I’m still not quite over the guilt of building software in this way. I don’t feel like I’ve earned the right to create something this good, in a field in which I have so little prior experience! At this point I’ve shown it to enough people in private that it felt wrong not to publish it for everyone else to see and learn from.

Games are also super low stakes. The worst that can happen is one of my silly game experiments suffers a bug.

This morning (via Hacker News) I found Steam Fans Are Begging for a No-AI Filter as Steam Next Fest Is Filled With Slop. I wouldn’t personally dream of submitting Battle Drones to an event like this—it’s still way too low effort to warrant consideration as a legitimate indie gaming project.

... but I can now see a path to vibe coded games like this being taken seriously. Battle Drones is fun, it looks good, it has innovative features (the multiplayer-over-audio thing is a first for an RTS as far as I can tell).
I’d love to see what someone with better taste than me and a driving passion to produce something truly exceptional could build!
A few other observations from this project:

Static HTML and JavaScript is a fantastic medium for games development. WebGL works great, and Three.js (and Phaser before it) are excellent platforms to build on that the current models know inside out.

This also lets them run as Progressive Web Apps—I didn’t ask for it, but Battle Drones works offline. I was able to play it on a plane despite never having directly installed it—my phone had it cached.
Giving Claude an OpenAI API key and telling it to generate images using OpenAI’s models works really well. It can view the images it has generated and iterate on the prompts.

Opus 5.5 is spectacular at 3D modeling using Three.js (and Blender, and no doubt other 3D applications as well). The same is true of GPT-6 Astra. They are absolutely capable of building models for 3D game projects.

For features like replay and multiplayer it’s useful to have a deterministic simulation engine. At one point Claude had to replace calls to Math.sin() and Math.cos() and friends with custom versions because different browsers (Chrome vs. Safari, for example) returned very slightly different numbers, desynchronizing the replay.

Opus 5.5 can write music! There are no audio files in this project—the soundtrack is entirely generated through code, varies across different maps, and even gets more intense as the battle heats up. See Scrimshaw Jukebox for a previous experiment with Claude for music composition.
I still can’t get over how well the prompt “Make it a LOT more fun” worked.
Tools are effectively free. I prompted up the Radio Probe, the Model browser, the Agent vs. Agent debug tool, and Claude Code built a bunch of tools for itself that I haven’t even explored myself.

Audio-based multiplayer between static HTML games works! I hope to see a whole lot more games use this same pattern—in digging around today I’ve not found much prior art beyond Siner by Alon Horesh and ggwave by Georgi Gerganov (also of llama.cpp fame).
Claude Code “Ultracode” burns tokens like there’s no tomorrow, but it can also solve complex problems (like adding audio-based multiplayer) from a single prompt.

I’m still not quite over the guilt of building software in this way. I don’t feel like I’ve earned the right to create something this good, in a field in which I have so little prior experience! At this point I’ve shown it to enough people in private that it felt wrong not to publish it for everyone else to see and learn from.

My obituary for programming (via) Jeremy Scheff poignantly captures the key loss caused by coding agents for career programmers who enjoyed the puzzle of developing code:

Programming turned into one of the greatest jobs you could imagine. You got paid to work on tricky little logic puzzles. The trickier the puzzle, the more you got paid. But even pretty simple puzzles were worth a lot of money because regular people just couldn't do it! No, they needed us. They would give us a problem and we would solve it the way we wanted. We set the strategy, we made the timeline, we defined what was and was not possible.
If you're a programmer who thrives on building working systems and doesn't care too deeply about the problems solved along the way, LLMs are the gift that keeps on giving.
If directly solving those problems was a big part of your enjoyment, the loss is very real.

articles.title: Laypeople support technical fields for technology, not art
articles.titleZh: Laypeople support technical fields for technology, not art
articles.summary: Laypeople support technical fields for technology, not art

blocks.text: Some people think that LLMs should not be used in technical fields like programming or mathematics, because those fields are actually art. True or not, this kind of argument is not going to be persuasive to the general population. The argument goes something1 like this:

It doesn’t matter how effective LLMs are at technical fields like programming or mathematics, because one of the essential values of those fields is that they’re art. While it looks to laypeople like these fields exist to solve practical problems, what they’re actually for is to produce works of beauty, or to express something distinctively human, or to spend time contemplating the infinite. Simply solving the problems misses the point in the same way that building an infinite poem generator would miss the point of poetry.

I agree that programming or mathematics can be beautiful. I remember being mildly awestruck at learning epsilon-delta proofs, and I have written a lot about the kind of software I think is elegant. Since there’s no clear definition of art or of aesthetics in general, it’s plausible to me that almost everything could have an artistic dimension to it.

All of this is compelling to software engineers, many of whom (like me) find some programs beautiful and are flattered to think of themselves as artists. But I suspect it’s spectacularly uncompelling to onlookers, because it undermines the implicit reasons that they have for supporting technical fields. Many people who are not programmers or mathematicians think of those fields like this:
I enjoy the fruits of technology: modern medicine, transport, mobile phones, and so on
While I don’t understand the exact relationship, I know that technical fields like mathematics and programming are essential to sustaining and advancing these technologies
Therefore I’m happy to respect and support mathematicians in their mysterious research work
And I’m broadly okay with2 software engineers drawing healthy salaries for the same reason

In other words, regular people3 think mathematicians (and to a lesser extent programmers) are valuable because they think science is valuable, and they think science is valuable because they think technology is valuable. They are willing to accept that technical fields can be art only insofar as that eventually helps researchers have the kind of creative insights that advance science: as Rikab sarcastically puts it, that advance the knowledge frontier.

If you go to those non-technical people and you say “LLMs can accelerate problem-solving in these fields, but I’m strongly against using them because the real point is to produce great art”, they will be very unhappy. They might reasonably feel cheated, in the same way as if they hired someone to renovate their kitchen who insisted in doing it all with hand tools in order to experience “the joy of creation”. This argument — we should stop using LLMs in technical fields because they’re art — is going to be even less compelling to technical employers.

Engineers and mathematicians who want to defend the artistic value of their field will need more compelling arguments4 than just appealing to the value of art. We will need to find some way to connect the value of art with the practical technological value that motivates public interest in our fields. For instance, we could argue that:
Great software products must rely on elegant abstractions, which need a human creative touch: simply piling on working code will hit a wall past a certain level of complexity
LLMs can solve problems, but actual progress in mathematics depends on creating new abstractions, which is a more creative task that LLMs are not yet good at
Progress in technical fields is uneven and relies upon inspiration, which needs creative hammock time and distinctively human understanding
LLMs can produce working software, but truly great software requires human inspiration5, and great software is what advances the field

I don’t know if I agree with all of these points. I haven’t yet seen an LLM-created codebase truly hit a wall (at least, not this year), and I don’t see a reason why LLMs should be incapable of creating new abstractions or having human-like inspirations. I also don’t think great products have to have great code: why wouldn’t workmanlike code in service of a great idea be enough? Does Fallingwater have to have beautifully installed6 insulation?

Still, any argument we make to our employers or the general public about art is going to have to try and make this case. Instead of saying that human-made technical work is valuable because it’s art, we need to make an affirmative case for why art can make technical work more effective. Otherwise we’re conceding the main reason why the general population thinks our work matters.

articles.titleZh: Barack Obama on the Trump Administration’s Intimidation Campaign Against Congresswoman Ilhan Omar
articles.summary: Barack Obama on the Trump Administration’s Intimidation Campaign Against Congresswoman Ilhan Omar

blocks.text:
It is a basic principle of American democracy that the government can’t selectively target individuals simply because of their political beliefs or what they say. But that’s exactly what the Trump Administration is doing to Congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota.

To understand why this is so appalling, it’s important to know the facts. Congresswoman Omar came to this country with her father when she was 12 years old. Five years later, her father became a naturalized citizen. If Ilhan had been 18 at the time, she would have had to apply for citizenship separately. But because she was 17, she became a naturalized citizen automatically.

Congresswoman Omar went on to graduate from college, work as a community organizer, become the first Somali-American legislator elected to public office in the U.S., and win a seat in Congress. There, she has been one of the Trump Administration’s fiercest critics, which has led the president to repeatedly single her out as someone who he believes does not belong in this country.

Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen. Federal agents have raided her home, confiscated personal records, and seized her phone — all to try and uncover a nonexistent smoking gun from 20 years ago that will somehow make their case.

Think about that. The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president. And it’s not the first time this has happened. Under President Trump, the Justice Department has repeatedly gone after those he considers his political enemies — from the Attorney General of New York, to the former head of the FBI, to members of the Federal Reserve.

In those cases, the prosecutions either stalled or were dismissed for having no basis in law, and the same is likely to happen in this case. But not before Congresswoman Omar’s life has been turned upside down, her legal bills have piled up, and she’s been forced to spend time fighting unsubstantiated charges instead of serving the people of Minnesota.

The fact that any president, or any administration, is willing to engage in such transparent efforts to intimidate someone should outrage all Americans, regardless of how they feel about Congresswoman Omar’s political views. Because if this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her — or that future presidents, in either party, won’t do the same.

blocks.text: Speaking of Ben Schlappig at One Mile at a Time, he had a post last week that I’ve been thinking a lot about. The gist:

American Airlines CEO Robert Isom appeared in court yesterday as
part of the current Department of Justice case. While being
questioned, the topic of JetBlue Mint came up, which is JetBlue’s
business class product. Isom claimed that he has never flown
JetBlue Mint, and doesn’t know if JetBlue Mint is lie-flat. He
then clarified that he understands that Mint is JetBlue’s domestic
first class, but “can’t speak to all the amenities they include.”
Here’s the part that I’ve been thinking about:

I’ve had the opportunity to interact with quite a few senior
airline executives over the years, and I find that their knowledge
about competitors is typically one extreme or the other:


Some airline executives literally couldn’t tell you the first
thing about their competitors, and have no knowledge of their
passenger experience, fleet, etc.
Some airline executives know literally everything about their
competitors, down to being able to tell you how many seats
competitors have on specific planes


I find there are very few executives who are just kind of in the
middle, as it’s pretty polarizing. Either they know virtually
everything about competitors, or nearly nothing. Without naming
any names, I’ll say that generally speaking there’s a high
correlation between airlines that have a great passenger
experience, and airlines that have executives that keep very close
tabs on the competition.

If you ask me, every CEO of a US airline offering a premium
product should have to fly JetBlue Mint, to see how good seats,
service, Wi-Fi, entertainment, food, and drinks, can be on a
domestic flight.
As someone who flies business class on American a few times per year, I am zero percent surprised that Isom doesn’t know or care about the experience flying American’s competitors.

The sentiment Schlappig expressed above isn’t airline-specific. I think it comes down to the classic idea of a “businessperson”. That an executive can just have a knack for “business”. That an MBA trains a would-be executive to run any sort of company. That’s probably the sort of executives who run most companies in most industries. But I don’t think it’s how excellent companies are led. Excellent companies, in any industry, seem to be led by executives who live and breathe whatever it is their companies do, and they stay up at night and wake up in the morning thinking about how to lead their industries in quality.

If the CEO’s primary perspective on the company is via spreadsheets — if it’s all just P&L to them — that company is not going to excel at quality. Or if they do excel at quality, they won’t for long.
★ Tuesday, 11 October 2022

The death of history's most successful publisher (permalink)

I published my first story in 1988, when I was 17 years old. Today, at 55, I've published more than 30 books, with three more coming in the next year or so. In the intervening years, I've spent a lot of time thinking and talking about publishing.

I've had plenty of opportunity to reflect on publishing: I've been a bookseller and worked in libraries, I wrote a column for Publishers Weekly, self-published a few books of my own, published the first-ever book licensed under Creative Commons, and broke several Kickstarter records for audiobook projects. But most of all, I've worked with publishing professionals: publicists, marketing directors, operations people, copyeditors, and, above all, editors.

My first novel editor was the magnificent Patrick Nielsen Hayden, who supported my publishing career from the very start, donating to help send me to the Clarion science fiction writers' workshop and inviting me to come read slush at Tor Books whenever I was in New York. Patrick didn't teach me everything I know about publishing, but he sure taught me a lot about publishing, and hardly a day goes by without my having cause to reflect on one of our many discussions over our decades-long professional and personal association.

Out of all the things I learned about publishing from Patrick, one truth stands out above all: publishing is "the act of making something public." Publishing may or may not involve editing, layout, printing, binding, marketing or other activities that we associate with publishing houses, but publishing always involves identifying a work, identifying an audience, and finding ways to connect that work to that audience.

This definition does a lot of useful work. For one thing, it locates publishing as part of the hard problem of human society, namely, "getting people to care about something that matters to you." Beyond publishing, this is the crux of politics, religion and commerce:
https://pluralistic.net/2021/07/04/self-publishing/

For another, this definition lets us understand that (for most of its existence) Google was the most successful publisher in human history. No other institution of any kind connected more works with more audiences. Lots of people have heard of Google's wildly unsuccessful motto "Don't be evil," but far fewer are familiar with Google's wildly successful mission statement, "organize the world's information and make it universally accessible and useful."

But all of that is in the past tense. With its AI projects – AI summaries, the Gemini chatbot – Google has abandoned the practice of "connecting works with audiences." Today, Google's function is to plunder all the works on the internet and chop them up and arrange them in an unimaginably vast, multidimensional array for the explicit purpose of preventing audiences from connecting with those works.

For most of its history, Google operated in a virtuous cycle with publishers whereby they allowed Google to crawl their sites and Google located audiences and connected them with the pages on those sites. Today, that cycle has turned vicious, with Google acting as a parasite that extracts value from the web's publishers and offers nothing in return.

This is entirely in keeping with the enshittification hypothesis: that once a platform is liberated from the disciplining forces of competition, regulation, labor and interoperability, it will squeeze its suppliers and users and harvest all the value for itself:
https://pluralistic.net/2023/01/21/potemkin-ai/#hey-guys

But AI represents a new phase in enshittification. Google has assayed enshittificatory gambits in the past, like deliberately worsening its search results in order to force you to search repeatedly, which gave the company more chances to show you ads:
https://pluralistic.net/2024/04/24/naming-names/#prabhakar-raghavan

But as sleazy as those gambits were, they were profitable. In some important sense, they were sustainable. Assuming Google could carry on indefinitely scamming its users in this way, they'd continue to bring in more cash than they spent, and continue to be the world's most successful publisher, connecting works and audiences (albeit in a deliberately degraded way).

Contrast this with AI, the money-losingest endeavor in the history of human civilization. Google is losing hundreds of billions of dollars on AI. The more AI Google does, the worse the company's financial footing becomes. If Google does this for long enough, it may cease to exist altogether. This collapse can only be prolonged by Google's ongoing extraction of value from web publishers, who no longer have their works connected with audiences via Google search results. Instead, Google usurps those audiences, shows them as many ads as it can, and still loses money in the bargain.

In Tim Wu's Age of Extraction, Wu lays out a thesis about how intermediaries – middlemen who perform a useful function connecting different groups, firms and individuals – are prone to developing "main character syndrome," abandoning their role as facilitators for others and abusing their position to make themselves the prime beneficiary of the transactions they facilitate:
https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/691177/the-age-of-extraction-by-tim-wu/

Google has a scorching case of main character syndrome, and nowhere is that more obvious than in its AI-fueled transformation into web-scale parasite. The fact that this gambit might well destroy Google and the publishers the company once served – rather than merely enshittifying search with worse results and more ads – makes the whole thing look more like a Mafia bust-out than the enshittification of the first half of the 2020s:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bust_Out
It's certainly an ignominious end for history's most successful publisher (as was).

The death of history's most successful publisher (permalink)

I published my first story in 1988, when I was 17 years old. Today, at 55, I've published more than 30 books, with three more coming in the next year or so. In the intervening years, I've spent a lot of time thinking and talking about publishing.

I've had plenty of opportunity to reflect on publishing: I've been a bookseller and worked in libraries, I wrote a column for Publishers Weekly, self-published a few books of my own, published the first-ever book licensed under Creative Commons, and broke several Kickstarter records for audiobook projects. But most of all, I've worked with publishing professionals: publicists, marketing directors, operations people, copyeditors, and, above all, editors.

My first novel editor was the magnificent Patrick Nielsen Hayden, who supported my publishing career from the very start, donating to help send me to the Clarion science fiction writers' workshop and inviting me to come read slush at Tor Books whenever I was in New York. Patrick didn't teach me everything I know about publishing, but he sure taught me a lot about publishing, and hardly a day goes by without my having cause to reflect on one of our many discussions over our decades-long professional and personal association.

Out of all the things I learned about publishing from Patrick, one truth stands out above all: publishing is "the act of making something public." Publishing may or may not involve editing, layout, printing, binding, marketing or other activities that we associate with publishing houses, but publishing always involves identifying a work, identifying an audience, and finding ways to connect that work to that audience.

This definition does a lot of useful work. For one thing, it locates publishing as part of the hard problem of human society, namely, "getting people to care about something that matters to you." Beyond publishing, this is the crux of politics, religion and commerce:
https://pluralistic.net/2021/07/04/self-publishing/

For another, this definition lets us understand that (for most of its existence) Google was the most successful publisher in human history. No other institution of any kind connected more works with more audiences. Lots of people have heard of Google's wildly unsuccessful motto "Don't be evil," but far fewer are familiar with Google's wildly successful mission statement, "organize the world's information and make it universally accessible and useful."

But all of that is in the past tense. With its AI projects – AI summaries, the Gemini chatbot – Google has abandoned the practice of "connecting works with audiences." Today, Google's function is to plunder all the works on the internet and chop them up and arrange them in an unimaginably vast, multidimensional array for the explicit purpose of preventing audiences from connecting with those works.

For most of its history, Google operated in a virtuous cycle with publishers whereby they allowed Google to crawl their sites and Google located audiences and connected them with the pages on those sites. Today, that cycle has turned vicious, with Google acting as a parasite that extracts value from the web's publishers and offers nothing in return.

This is entirely in keeping with the enshittification hypothesis: that once a platform is liberated from the disciplining forces of competition, regulation, labor and interoperability, it will squeeze its suppliers and users and harvest all the value for itself:
https://pluralistic.net/2023/01/21/potemkin-ai/#hey-guys

But AI represents a new phase in enshittification. Google has assayed enshittificatory gambits in the past, like deliberately worsening its search results in order to force you to search repeatedly, which gave the company more chances to show you ads:
https://pluralistic.net/2024/04/24/naming-names/#prabhakar-raghavan

But as sleazy as those gambits were, they were profitable. In some important sense, they were sustainable. Assuming Google could carry on indefinitely scamming its users in this way, they'd continue to bring in more cash than they spent, and continue to be the world's most successful publisher, connecting works and audiences (albeit in a deliberately degraded way).

Contrast this with AI, the money-losingest endeavor in the history of human civilization. Google is losing hundreds of billions of dollars on AI. The more AI Google does, the worse the company's financial footing becomes. If Google does this for long enough, it may cease to exist altogether. This collapse can only be prolonged by Google's ongoing extraction of value from web publishers, who no longer have their works connected with audiences via Google search results. Instead, Google usurps those audiences, shows them as many ads as it can, and still loses money in the bargain.

In Tim Wu's Age of Extraction, Wu lays out a thesis about how intermediaries – middlemen who perform a useful function connecting different groups, firms and individuals – are prone to developing "main character syndrome," abandoning their role as facilitators for others and abusing their position to make themselves the prime beneficiary of the transactions they facilitate:
https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/691177/the-age-of-extraction-by-tim-wu/

Google has a scorching case of main character syndrome, and nowhere is that more obvious than in its AI-fueled transformation into web-scale parasite. The fact that this gambit might well destroy Google and the publishers the company once served – rather than merely enshittifying search with worse results and more ads – makes the whole thing look more like a Mafia bust-out than the enshittification of the first half of the 2020s:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bust_Out
It's certainly an ignominious end for history's most successful publisher (as was).

blocks.text: This is a charming and funny book all about the various ways humans have promoted fake medical cures in exchange for money.

Despite the grim (and occasionally distressing) subject matter, the tone remains light and poppy throughout. There are lots of snarky asides (especially about the fake medical practitioners) and a real appreciation for the bizarre. It's fun the whole way through, although sometimes at the expense of people who perhaps didn't know better than to trust charlatans.
One thing that is constantly brought back is how it can be hard to determine what is patent nonsense and what is a bone fide cure:
Prevent blood clotting: Extract mucus from the intestinal membranes of slaughtered pigs or from the lungs of slaughtered cows. Inject. (heparin)
Is that any more believable than injecting goat testicles to cure impotence?
It also brings to light how squeamish we can be, especially when faced with unusual medical procedures:
We borrow other people’s wombs for surrogacy. And yet, plenty of people squirm at the idea of breastmilk banks. We are a society of contradictions.

The eBook is beautifully formatted. For once, images are in-line with the text! Usually in books of this sort, publishers treat the eBook like a mass-market paperback and stick the illustrations at the end.
It ends rather abruptly, after taking us through light, electricity, colour therapy, animal magnetism, and a couple of dozen other "cure-alls"

Sadly, there are no references or footnotes. While I have no reason to doubt the veracity of the claims, for a book about scientific misinformation and malpractice, I'd've expected a way to find out more information.

blocks.text: Should domains last forever? That’s not a new question for me, but it’s one that I’ve been thinking more about lately, especially since I ended up writing a story recently that posed this exact question.

Over at the new publication GraveSite, which covers the concept of death and grief with a reporter’s eye, I posed a question I’ve thought a lot about over the years: How can you keep a person’s digital identity alive even if their physical identity is long gone? For corporate entities this is actually reasonably easy—succession plans and all that, ensuring someone is paying the bills long-term.

But people aren‘t corporations, and business structures like domain registrars and web hosts often treat us as consumers. Which means that when we aren’t around to consume, and to pay money in exchange for that consumption, we’re going to be the first to lose our digital plot in the ground. There’s no internet cemetery, and we have a relatively limited number of archives that can hold our digital histories.

Which means that, when we go offline, so will our digital identities, eventually. It’ll take longer, but that credit card isn’t going to pay for itself. If you’re a writer or creative, this is a real risk, and the answers for solving this simply aren’t very good.
My piece goes over some of the novel solutions out there, including a nonprofit initiative to essentially take ownership of websites and pay the bills in your absence.

I’m happy with the piece, but don’t want to spoil it, so I’ll simply encourage you to read. But I wanted to spend a second thinking about a the second-order effects of this: If domains last forever, at what point do we need to start over?

This was an argument I heard from a couple of readers about this topic. There’s a finite number of domains—at what point are the domains already here going to crowd out people that left a long time ago. I own the domain erniesmith.net that I use to promote my freelance work; if I decided to sell it to a service that aims to keep a domain around “forever,” am I screwing over later generations of Ernie Smiths?

It’s hard to say, but I do think it speaks to a longer-term architecture problem that the internet will eventually face, a crossroads as our domain owners die out, the domain maybe not being relevant anymore but their websites certainly having some value. And maybe the solution to this problem is to create new systems for distributing information online that don’t necessarily rely on domains.

One commenter on my post, Alex Russell (a former Google Chrome engineer now working on Microsoft Edge), pointed to the idea of Web Packages, a concept where websites could be distributed in full without the need for any attached domain or even expected online access.

It was an idea that originated with the Chrome team, but found little to no uptake with other browser-makers, eventually falling into the abyss of Web standards obscurities. (The project currently lives with the Web Incubator Community Group (WICG).) It arguably deserves to be revisited as the problem of dead websites and dead owners becomes a bigger problem. For one thing, it helps to resolve some of the bigger, more annoying problems with old websites—that they’re often required to be static when they’ve fallen into disuse, that they often don’t support https like modern sites do, and that they can carry latent security issues, much like how an old book can grow dust and mold if not managed properly. (In fact, one of the listed uses for web packages is to create an easy-to-distribute format for researching security exploits.)

Should the domain system itself be seen as temporary? Should we treat old websites more like books whose volumes can be picked up at will when all is said and done? That’s a provocative idea, and one that I think deserves more discussion in the current climate.

But one thing I’ll say is that our system is completely upside down if your website stands a better chance of being around in 100 years if it’s a Facebook profile or a forgotten Blogger or LiveJournal site than if you put in the work to carefully put it on the internet yourself.

Anyway, I look forward to talking about these issues with the GraveSite team on October 27, when I’ll be taking part in their HellFireside Chat on digital death. If this topic at all appeals to you, hope to see you there.

As the Mullenweg turns: Get ready for some drama, folks. Fortune has a feature explaining what, exactly, happened with Matt Mullenweg last month when he very briefly was booted from his CEO role with Automattic. As you might guess, it has to do with the ongoing WP Engine mess.

A quick shout-out to friend of Tedium Sean Malseed, a.k.a. Action Retro, who publicly discussed his health issues with his audience. translations: Should domains last forever? That’s not a new question for me, but it’s one that I’ve been thinking more about lately, especially since I ended up writing a story recently that posed this exact question.

Over at the new publication GraveSite, which covers the concept of death and grief with a reporter’s eye, I posed a question I’ve thought a lot about over the years: How can you keep a person’s digital identity alive even if their physical identity is long gone? For corporate entities this is actually reasonably easy—succession plans and all that, ensuring someone is paying the bills long-term.

But people aren‘t corporations, and business structures like domain registrars and web hosts often treat us as consumers. Which means that when we aren’t around to consume, and to pay money in exchange for that consumption, we’re going to be the first to lose our digital plot in the ground. There’s no internet cemetery, and we have a relatively limited number of archives that can hold our digital histories.

Which means that, when we go offline, so will our digital identities, eventually. It’ll take longer, but that credit card isn’t going to pay for itself. If you’re a writer or creative, this is a real risk, and the answers for solving this simply aren’t very good.
My piece goes over some of the novel solutions out there, including a nonprofit initiative to essentially take ownership of websites and pay the bills in your absence.

I’m happy with the piece, but don’t want to spoil it, so I’ll simply encourage you to read. But I wanted to spend a second thinking about a the second-order effects of this: If domains last forever, at what point do we need to start over?

This was an argument I heard from a couple of readers about this topic. There’s a finite number of domains—at what point are the domains already here going to crowd out people that left a long time ago. I own the domain erniesmith.net that I use to promote my freelance work; if I decided to sell it to a service that aims to keep a domain around “forever,” am I screwing over later generations of Ernie Smiths?

It’s hard to say, but I do think it speaks to a longer-term architecture problem that the internet will eventually face, a crossroads as our domain owners die out, the domain maybe not being relevant anymore but their websites certainly having some value. And maybe the solution to this problem is to create new systems for distributing information online that don’t necessarily rely on domains.

One commenter on my post, Alex Russell (a former Google Chrome engineer now working on Microsoft Edge), pointed to the idea of Web Packages, a concept where websites could be distributed in full without the need for any attached domain or even expected online access.

It was an idea that originated with the Chrome team, but found little to no uptake with other browser-makers, eventually falling into the abyss of Web standards obscurities. (The project currently lives with the Web Incubator Community Group (WICG).) It arguably deserves to be revisited as the problem of dead websites and dead owners becomes a bigger problem. For one thing, it helps to resolve some of the bigger, more annoying problems with old websites—that they’re often required to be static when they’ve fallen into disuse, that they often don’t support https like modern sites do, and that they can carry latent security issues, much like how an old book can grow dust and mold if not managed properly. (In fact, one of the listed uses for web packages is to create an easy-to-distribute format for researching security exploits.)

Should the domain system itself be seen as temporary? Should we treat old websites more like books whose volumes can be picked up at will when all is said and done? That’s a provocative idea, and one that I think deserves more discussion in the current climate.

But one thing I’ll say is that our system is completely upside down if your website stands a better chance of being around in 100 years if it’s a Facebook profile or a forgotten Blogger or LiveJournal site than if you put in the work to carefully put it on the internet yourself.

Anyway, I look forward to talking about these issues with the GraveSite team on October 27, when I’ll be taking part in their HellFireside Chat on digital death. If this topic at all appeals to you, hope to see you there.

Something funny happened a little while ago: I read about FreshRSS, and it
sounded nice, so I installed it on a server and started using it. That would
not have happened a year ago, but then again, a year ago I didn’t have any NixOS
servers.

For the past few years, my rss feeds have lived locally on my phone only.
There was a good idea behind that11 I can mostly take time to read when I’m
away from my computer anyway., but it never quite worked in practice. For one,
many things are easier to read on a larger screen. But it was also brittle to
trust a phone app to manage the read/unread status of thousands of articles
across a hundred feeds.22 In particular, when I switched to a different phone
I could migrate all feeds to it, but the read/unread status was lost along the
way. What I really wanted was a server-side feed aggregator. This is software
that runs on a server, manages rss feeds, and then I can read the rss feeds
either through a web interface, or through client applications. I’ve wanted that
for a while, but I’ve never taken the step, because it would be yet another side
project to maintain the deployment of.

But now, with some NixOS experience, adding a working FreshRSS configuration
(including backups) took 9 lines of Nix code33 Plus a dozen more lines for the
nginx reverse proxy configuration. It got a little complicated because I wanted
to proxy_pass from a specific location block which required rewriting cookie
paths. But that’s a me problem, not a NixOS problem.. That installation has
just hands-off worked for the past few months. If or when that server breaks, I
can spin up a new one running the exact same configuration, probably in
something like 15 minutes. When we can do something like that, there is
literally no reason to not just try the new software.
Contrast this against how FreshRSS is installed outside of NixOS. Then we’d
download and extract an archive to the right location;
configure permissions according to instructions;
install nginx and php-fpm with necessary extra dependencies to the server;
configure php-fpm pools and make nginx pass requests through to php-fpm;
set up Let’s Encrypt certificates;
set up backups; and

hopefully remember how to do all the above if something breaks and we need to
reinstall FreshRSS on a new or upgraded server later.

Of course, the FreshRSS project provides a container image which would shorten
the process a little bit. It purports to set up Apache with mod_php and
configure them the right way. Then we’d only need to configure backups, create a
systemd service that runs the container, and manage nginx as a tls terminating
reverse proxy in front of that, because the container image reasonably does not
come with tls support. This is still stuff to remember, and there’s also no
guarantee the same thing works six months down the line when reinstalling,
unless we wrote down which exact container image we downloaded.44 It does not
help to build the container image from source, because two builds from the same
Dockerfile separated by time can result in rather different container images.

I have mentioned before how much I dislike maintaining side projects. That
includes my own code, but also self-hosted services developed by someone else.
I’m okay with a few minutes of maintenance here and there, but having to
schedule hours of uninterrupted work to upgrade something, or spending any
amount of time at all on emergency maintenance, really kills my desire to work
with computers.

You’d think someone of my disposition would be deep into configuration
management, container orchestration, or both, but no. I have made honest
attempts with CFEngine, Ansible, podman, and k3s but none of them improved my
installation/configuration/deployment experience significantly over (a)
carefully writing things down, and sometimes (b) turning those careful notes
into a shell script performing a sequence of ssh commands.55 Yes, this is
essentially reinventing Ansible – but less brittle. It won’t break the next time
someone glances sideways at pip. The drawback of the shell script is that it
often ends up relying on assumptions that become invalid with time, or when it
is used in a different environment. A NixOS configuration reads a lot like the
careful instructions to myself, except they’re executable and they produce the
same result every time.

blocks.text: If you liked this piece, you should subscribe to my premium newsletter, and you can subscribe on the following links: $70 a year, $18 a quarter, or $7 a month.

In return, you get a weekly premium newsletter that dives deep into the finances of the AI bubble. Over the past few months, I’ve published a two part guide to the world of AI debt, an analysis of the (dubious) impact of generative AI on the global economy, deep analyses of the biggest players in the AI infrastructure space like NVIDIA (part one and two) and Oracle (part one and two), how OpenAI will eventually kill Oracle, and how venture capital is killing itself.
Friday’s piece will be the Hater's Guide to Blackstone — one of the most loathsome companies in existence, and one that’s staked its entire existence on the AI bubble.

If you want to get in touch — and especially if you have any juicy information about Anthropic, OpenAI, Blackstone or any other companies in the AI bubble — hit me up on Signal at ezitron.76. I’m also on IB on your Bloomberg Terminal.
Soundtrack: Royal Blood — Pull Me Through
At the end of July, Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok gave a blunt warning to the Washington Post:
“This AI thing better work out because if it doesn’t ... we’re going to have a problem,” said Torsten Slok, chief economist at investment firm Apollo Global Management.
Today, I’m going to quantify exactly how difficult it will be for the “AI thing” to “work out.”
As I’ve said before:

…everybody wants to make the AI bubble really complex, it’s actually super simple: hundreds of billions of dollars are being invested to make single-digit billions of dollars maybe, some day, if AI data centers actually get built at scale and OpenAI and Anthropic can afford to pay for their compute.

The theoreticals and hypotheticals of this industry are so powerful that they’ve created one of the (if not the) largest equities bubbles in modern history, all heavily-centralized around the valuations of a handful of names related to the so-called AI trade, which translates to “buying or selling stuff to do with AI GPUs.”
The AI Trade Is A Global Concentration Risk, With Growth Dependent On Endless Capex Spend and VC-Backed GPU Rentals

This has led to the single-highest inflow of foreign investments into US equities in history — larger than the Dot-Com Bubble, the leadup to the Great Financial Crisis, and even the dying gasps of the Zero Interest Free Era in 2021, per Apollo:

However you might hand-wave away the AI bubble’s economic issues by saying it’s “just like the Dot-Com Bubble” — when the NASDAQ 100 fell 77% from its peak — the consequences are now global, at a scale unseen in history, flowing into both direct stocks and indices.

As of typing this sentence, NVIDIA alone makes up 11.31% of the NASDAQ 100, with the combined weight of NVIDIA, Google, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Broadcom, Micron, AMD and CoreWeave representing about 46.5% of the index’s value, or 39.3% of the entire 3000-company NASDAQ composite.
These same names — replacing CoreWeave with Oracle — represent around 28.9% of the value of the S&P 500.

To sustain the valuation of these stocks — let alone continue growing — will require every company involved to either spend or make hundreds of billions of dollars in perpetuity, increasing every single quarter, without fail. This will come from either selling ever-increasing amounts of AI chips and related hardware, or buying and using them to generate revenue either through rentals or building their own software products.

While the centralization was more severe at the top of the Dot-Com era NASDAQ — with Cisco, Intel and Microsoft accounting for roughly 74% — the total value of the index was a mere $1.82 trillion ($3.58 trillion adjusted for inflation).
Today’s top three — NVIDIA, Google and Microsoft — account for around 29% of the NASDAQ 100, for a total market capitalization of $13.5 trillion.
I’m afraid things only get worse.
Retail Investors Own 10% Of The Market, With 38%+ US Household Wealth Held In Stocks, and Hold at least 22.4% of NVIDIA and 21.7% of Microsoft’s Traded Stock

Per Goldman Sachs (via Reuters), "...equity gains have been the dominant driver of household wealth accumulation ​and the main contributor to a positive wealth ​effect on consumer spending," and per data from the Fed, corporate equities accounted for 37.9% of all household wealth in Q2 2026, the highest number on record since Q4 2000.
Economist Paul Kedrosky told me it might actually be higher:

Americans are near records in terms of equity exposure, over 50% [as in number of Americans holding stocks], ahead of real estate for the first time since WWII — and Americans are at record levels in terms of equities as a percentage of their liquid net worth — over 60%.

While the Fed’s data only goes back to Q4 2000, corporate equities as a share of household wealth only sat at 25.9% ($11.5 trillion, or $22.7 trillion adjusted for inflation), back at a time when total household wealth sat at $44.4 trillion, or about $85.2 trillion in today’s money. In Q2 2026, total household wealth sits at about $195.8 trillion, with corporate equities sitting at roughly $74 trillion, or roughly 86.8% of the entire US household wealth 26 years ago.

Retails are also making up an historically-large amount of the volume of trades on the market, per Bloomberg Intelligence, making up 20.3% of trading in 2026 to date, approaching the dangerous heights of the worst excesses of the end of the Zero Interest Rate Policy era.

Retail investors also directly own about 29% of Amazon’s, 26.2% of NVIDIA’s, 22.6% of AMD’s, 21.8% of Microsoft’s, and 18.6% of Meta’s stocks, though these numbers are not inclusive of index funds like SPY or QQQ (a fund tied to the NASDAQ). In totality, retail investors own equity assets (at least as of May) equivalent to about 10% of the market.
In fact, Goldman Sachs had retail volumes significantly higher:

In a note to clients, analyst Daniel Chavez explained that Goldman Sachs trading desk data shows retail volumes have risen 28% since mid-April, with a basket of retail-favorite stocks tracked by the firm gaining 29% over the same period.

By comparison, Dot-Com era retail trading was much, much lower — less than 2% of the NYSE’s trading volume according to the University of Michigan’s Alicia J. Davis in a paper that begins with the phrase “the American retail investor is dying.”

When all of this is over, I think retail investors might wish they were dead, as they directly own somewhere in the region of $4.65 trillion worth of NVIDIA, Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Meta, Broadcom, AMD, Micron, Oracle, and CoreWeave stocks. The number is likely much smaller than the true exposure retail investors have, as it isn’t inclusive of investments in index funds.

Sidenote: For some comparison, the total market capitalization of Microsoft, Cisco and Intel on March 10, 2000 (the peak of the market) was around $1.36 trillion. Another point is that, unlike 2000, retail investors have easy access to exotic securities contracts that weren’t previously available (or, if they were available, were expensive or otherwise obscured from the casual view of most retail investors), and that have the potential to amplify any potential losses.  RobinHood, for example, allows retail investors to buy event contracts (where “investors” speculate on an event with a yes/no outcome), to trade futures, to short stock, and to invest on margin, or with borrowed money. All of this can be done (assuming the investor meets the criteria to access these products) with a few taps on a phone, effectively eliminating the friction associated with making a potentially life-altering financial decision.
Sidenote: CoreWeave isn’t on the S&P 500 and Oracle isn’t on the NASDAQ, just for comprehensiveness.

On April 14, 2000, the NASDAQ composite dropped 9.67% and the S&P 500 5.78%, with a little under 97% of the S&P 500 constituents falling on the day, per TIME and The Washington Post, led by hot inflation numbers and overall anxiety over the tech sector’s valuations:

There were virtually no exceptions to the decline. The correction, analysts said, was taking no prisoners. The crash came at the end of an extraordinary week, where volatility and huge drops were the rule rather than the exception. And market analysts said they expect the declines to continue next week--and possibly in the coming weeks and months--as overvalued stocks come down to earth.
Yet the Post had one telling quote, emphasis mine:

Market momentum--which has trended up for the longest bull market in history for much of the past decade--has now turned down. The recognition that many technology stocks can't possibly grow quickly enough to merit the heights they achieved through momentum investing may have pierced the bubble of overvaluation in recent weeks, analysts said, as momentum changed direction. That turnaround has sent the Nasdaq composite index down 35 percent since its high on March 10.

While it seems unlikely, a drop of around 20% across NVIDIA, Amazon, Google, Meta, Broadcom, AMD, Oracle, Micron, and CoreWeave would have the same effect as the entire market downturn on the worst day of the Dot-Com Bubble crash.
In truth, it wouldn’t even have to be that bad.
Per CNN Moneyline News Hour transcript from April 14, 2000, Qualcomm fell 21%, Yahoo fell 20%, Intel a little over 10%, and Microsoft a mere 5% — and that’s all it took to make the market bottom out.
Brief NVIDIA selloffs have already caused big market declines:

On Jan 27, 2025, NVIDIA dropped 17%, its worst daily percentage loss (per Forbes) since March 2020, with the S&P 500 dropping 1.5% and the NASDAQ 3.1%, though its share of the S&P 500 at the time was about 1.9% smaller.
On June 5, 2026, NVIDIA dropped about 6.2%, with the NASDAQ ending the day down 4.18% and the S&P 500 down 2.64%.
Anyway, remember that quote about momentum investing, overvaluations and growth? Here’s a quote from Bloomberg from last week (October 14), emphasis mine:

Chipmakers fell for an eighth straight day, the longest slide since 2008, on worries over whether the AI infrastructure buildout has outrun the ability of firms to get a return on their investments. CoreWeave Inc., a cloud-computing services provider whose bonds recently hit levels that typically signal distress, sank 12%. The S&P 500 lost 1.1%. Oil climbed, weighing on Treasuries.
And here’s another quote from CNN from a day later, emphasis mine:

The global retreat in chip stocks followed a sharp sell-off on Wall Street on Wednesday, after a strong US inflation report bolstered worries that rising interest rates will make it more expensive for companies to fund AI investments. Many AI companies are already heavily indebted.
History may not repeat, but it rhymes. Every problem that burst the Dot-Com Bubble is here, but it’s worse, bigger and uglier, with global contagion risk that I basically never see discussed.

For example, the ongoing equity price of TSMC on the Taiwanese Stock Exchange makes up about 40% of the entire market, with the ODMs that have seen booming earnings making AI servers for hyperscalers representing another 3% or so. On The Tokyo Stock Exchange, the combined weight of SoftBank, RAM maker Kioxia, and the two major banks (SMBC and MUFG) backing AI data centers make up approximately 11.24% of the TOPIX Index. Samsung and SK Hynix, both of whom have seen remarkable RAM sales (see my Hater’s Guide To The Memory Crisis for more), make up more than 50% of the entire value of Korea’s KOSPI.
Their elevated valuations come from a belief that they’ll grow in perpetuity, much like the American markets.
And let’s be clear about something: all it takes is the vibe souring to the point that people lose faith in the AI trade for everything to start to collapse.
So, what will it take to keep the party going?
The answer is simple: perpetual, parabolic growth in both AI revenues and AI capex.
Gartner Says We Have More Compute Capacity Than We Have Demand, and 80% Of Neoclouds Will Be Dead By 2030
Per CNBC, well, exactly what I’ve been saying, emphasis mine:

“At the moment, we have more compute capacity than we have demand, and we have a lot of the tokens and processing power being given away in freemium solutions,” [Gartner’s John Lovelock] told CNBC. “Everyone in the AI race is running for a last-man standing position. Pretty much every market that Gartner is tracking in our AI race is likely to collapse down to a duopoly.”Neoclouds would not be going out of business en masse, Lovelock reiterated, but could be subject to consolidation, such as takeovers and mergers. As a result of their profitability analysis, Gartner predicted last week that 80% of neoclouds, which are AI-dedicated computing power providers, could cease functioning as independent companies.
Oh!
Are…are you sure about that? Isn’t AI the biggest, most hugest thing ever? It’s transformative! It’ll change everything! Aren’t we all excited-

Lovelock also said Monday that AI is a technology as opposed to a market, comparing it to table salt that will be sprinkled into existing commercial operations rather than creating an inherently new field in which companies will sell differentiated and competing products.
Okay, well, check out Doctor Doom over here, I bet he’s gonna be so surprised when those profitable returns come in-
In their Wednesday report, Gartner researchers found that overall “AI revenue will be insufficient to support profitable returns on all planned AI capital expenditures” between 2027 and 2030.
Well, at least there’s a diverse revenue base for GPU sales-OH MY GOD!
NVIDIA and Broadcom’s Continued Growth Is Contingent On Hyperscaler and Neocloud GPU/TPU Sales, Which Is Contingent On Debt and AI Revenues

NVIDIA has guided to a 70% increase in its next fiscal year — I assume FY2028, starting February 2027 — or over $670 billion in annual revenue, over three times its FY 2026 sales, with said sales dependent on whether Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Oracle, Meta, SpaceX (who collectively make up 50% to 60% of NVIDIA’s data center revenues), and the various neoclouds like CoreWeave, Nebius, and Nscale keep buying more of them every quarter, or at the very least that a willing vessel can step in to pick up the slack if they stop. If demand wavers, NVIDIA, Broadcom, Micron, AMD, and any associated silicon or hardware counterparties will see their revenue growth stumble, which will have a brutal knock-on effect on their stocks.

NVIDIA already has its own revenue concentration problem — 44% of its first half FY2027 revenues came from three customers, and in Q2 FY2027, 70% of its accounts receivables were from three customers, with 16% of its revenues coming from one. One. How is this not more worrying to people?

Anyway, to buy those GPUs (or TPUs, in Broadcom’s case), everyone outside of Microsoft will have to raise tens of billions of dollars of debt at a time when underlying interest rates are growing and the overall debt markets have chilled around AI data center debt.

Said chill comes from the world finally waking up to what I said in March 2025 — that CoreWeave is a time bomb of expensive debt that’s now selling off as people realize that making any of its supposed $104 billion in backlog (at least 50% of which is OpenAI and Anthropic) will require, per UBS, about $102 billion in debt in the next three years. CoreWeave’s long-dated bonds (by which I mean maturing in 2031) had an effective yield of as much as 16% in the last week.
AI Debt Is Becoming Too Expensive To Handle, With Many Bonds Secured By GPUs and Infrastructure With Questionable Post-Bubble Value

With endless delays and hundreds of billions of dollars of chips sitting in storage, AI data centers have dramatically turned from the panacea for all infrastructure investment to fixed-income nightmare fuel. For whatever reason, nobody thought that lending hundreds of billions of dollars to a selection of different dodgy SPVs and neoclouds to build the world’s most ambitious infrastructure projects was a problem until, well, everybody, per the WSJ:

There has been a surge in issuance of bonds to finance the construction of data centers for AI computing. This year through Oct. 16, data-center issuers have raised more than $100 billion in the U.S.-dollar bond market, or about 25% of AI-related gross issuance in U.S. currency, according to data from Dealogic and Goldman Sachs credit research analysts. That is up from around 16% the prior year.
Per the Journal, this debt heavily relies on both the continued value of the data center and critical IT gear and whether the bloody thing actually gets built:

The recent AI data center bonds typically have structures that are different from a company’s bonds. They can be secured by the data center being built, while corporate debt is unsecured. How much security that provides, though, also rests on the completion of the data center, and on the value of the data center to another tenant. Effectively, investors are betting that overall demand for data infrastructure means the data center will be of use to someone, even if the current tenant runs into trouble.

In other words, the value of that data center debt is heavily contingent on whether the underlying assets retain their value, which in turn is contingent on whether there are customers that exist. For whatever reason, nobody wants to consider the most obvious problem: that if one customer can’t pay, other customers can’t pay, and if other customers can’t pay, there’s going to be less demand for AI data centers in general, which means there will be a glut of data center infrastructure, which will mean those assets you intend to resell if everything goes poorly won’t be worth as much.
I sure hope that financial institutions have a plan…

“With a data-center bond, you’re underwriting assets, and our view has been that when it gets completed, that can be a meaningful catalyst for spreads to compress,” says Andrew Keches, who is tech, media and telecom credit analyst and head of high-yield research at Barclays.

Oh okay, the problem with overly-expensive AI data center debt is simply that the markets will feel better when the underlying data centers (which are overwhelmingly delayed) get built? Awesome! It’s just that simple! I’m sure somebody out there will deal with the massive delays for the talent, materials and power connections necessary to complete them!

The fundamental disconnection between the perception of AI growth inflating the value of hyperscaler stocks and the worrying fact that we don’t really know exactly how much AI revenue they make means that the S&P 500 and NASDAQ are held up by a kind of childish excitement that will, at some point, turn to existential fear.

I went into significantly more detail about it in my premium piece about how AI Isn’t Too Big To Fail.

The underlying weakness of the AI trade is that it isn’t really related to anything other than NVIDIA and the hyperscalers’ earnings.

We don’t know how many GPUs are in operation, we don’t know how much money the hyperscalers make from using them or renting them, we don’t know how many active gigawatts of AI capacity they have, we don’t know their actual customer concentration outside of analyst estimates, we don’t really know how much people pay to rent GPUs, and we don’t even know how much it costs to run a GPU on an hourly basis.

OpenAI and Anthropic are horrifyingly unprofitable, deeply unstable, and as I’ve discussed, 80% of their revenues come from companies that literally can’t afford to pay them, and yet the markets never react, because this information doesn’t really matter as long as the right numbers keep going up.

The fundamental disconnection between the perception of AI growth inflating the value of hyperscaler stocks and the worrying fact that we don’t really know exactly how much AI revenue they make means that the S&P 500 and NASDAQ are held up by a kind of childish excitement that will, at some point, turn to existential fear.
