The AI bubble was inflated by hyperscaler revenue growth (without any disclosure of AI revenue) and NVIDIA’s GPU sales, meaning that the moment one of those slows, everybody freaks out. The US government cannot bail out NVIDIA, Microsoft, Google, Amazon, CoreWeave or Meta’s future misses of analyst expectations, nor can it cover every single bankrupt data center, nor can it bail out investor sentiment when it realizes the AI “boom” was yet another tech-based bust. I went into significantly more detail about it in my premium piece about how AI Isn’t Too Big To Fail.

Remember: even with the bank bailout in 2008, the market still crumbled, and that was before we had over $40 trillion in debt, stubborn inflation, and a stock market that has fundamentally disconnected from reality.
The underlying weakness of the AI trade is that it isn’t really related to anything other than NVIDIA and the hyperscalers’ earnings.

We don’t know how many GPUs are in operation, we don’t know how much money the hyperscalers make from using them or renting them, we don’t know how many active gigawatts of AI capacity they have, we don’t know their actual customer concentration outside of analyst estimates, we don’t really know how much people pay to rent GPUs, and we don’t even know how much it costs to run a GPU on an hourly basis.

OpenAI and Anthropic are horrifyingly unprofitable, deeply unstable, and as I’ve discussed, 80% of their revenues come from companies that literally can’t afford to pay them, and yet the markets never react, because this information doesn’t really matter as long as the right numbers keep going up.

This is why Anthropic’s IPO travails are so profoundly dangerous for the AI trade. Investors are now suggesting that it prices its IPO at $1.5 trillion, meaning a significantly lower payoff for investors and much less capital raised on listing, meaning that it will have to take on more and more debt — like its 10% interest chip financing deal with Broadcom and Blackstone — that will provide a brutal education in what a high-burn-rate, negative-EBITDA company really looks like when you remove the layers of annualized run rates and hype.
And, per Irrational Analysis, Anthropic’s investor day didn’t go particularly well:

Broadly speaking, coding ARR has plateaued, or at least slowed significantly.OpenAI seems to have no plan, as Sam struggles to raise a new private round at $1.4T valuation. Middle East investors (of all people lol) are pushing back on the valuation.Anthropic apparently thinks bio (drug discovery) is the next big market for them. Yes, the most regulated and slow-to-revenue industry is what will fund all those "compute commitments”.I know several people who were at the private Antrhopic (sic) buyside investor day last week. It was apparently a shitshow. Nobody asked an intelligent question. Anthropic was vague and gave little information. Original valuation plan was $2T, dropped to $1.6-$1.8T, and has been dropped again to $1.5T allegedly… in less than 10 days.
Any further delays to Anthropic’s IPO will be somewhere between catastrophic and fatal, and at this point I think it’s fair to question whether it ever makes it to the public markets.

If it does, a $1.5 trillion valuation would spell disaster for OpenAI, which has (as mentioned above) been trying to raise $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Closing that round will be difficult to impossible at that price even without Anthropic’s drooping numbers, and if it somehow IPOs at something approaching $1 trillion, I have no idea how Clammy Sammy and OpenAI make it out of this one alive.
And really, does any of this look like the future? Does any of this feel like the next industrial revolution?
Or does it feel like the run-up to another burst bubble and resulting financial crisis?

The difference here is that AI has, for the most part, been sold as a panacea for the rich and powerful — a way to control, to steal, to acquire and to expand, to take and take and take as they always have, occasionally vaguely muttering something about “abundance” as both the media and financial institutions help force through yet another doomed cycle of “innovation.”

The people to blame are the tech CEOs — Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, Sundar Pichai, Andy Jassy, Elon Musk, Hock Tan, Jensen Huang, Sanjay Mehrotra to name a few — and the financiers that have helped them pump this bubble, with the worst of them being that rat fuck Stephen A. Schwarzman, CEO of Blackstone, a private equity (or “alternative asset”) firm that has funded basically every name I just wrote down on some level, funded by everyone from the Saudis to the California state pension system.
This week’s premium will be the Hater’s Guide To Blackstone, a company that vibrates with evil, and has staked its entire future on whether AI works out.
It’s a stupid fucking bet from an evil fucking company, and I can’t wait to tell you all about it on Friday.

blocks.text: Epyx was one of the most celebrated and prolific software publishers for 8-bit home computers, especially Atari and Commodore, and, to a lesser degree, Apple. But they struggled to transition to newer platforms and that ultimately led to bankruptcy, on October 19, 1989.
Early role-playing strategy games from Epyx

Initially Epyx was called Automated Simulations and its first product was a space-themed war game called Starfleet Orion written in PET Basic for the Commodore PET. They quickly ported it to the Apple II and TRS-80 as well, and followed it up in 1979 with Invasion Orion, which included a computer-controlled opponent.

The next game wasn’t a simulation, requiring a new brand name. Epyx was an appropriate name for a dungeon crawl roleplaying game called Temple of Apshai. Initially released in August 1979 for the TRS-80 and Commodore PET, Epyx ported it to the Apple II, Atari 800, IBM PC, Commodore 64 and VIC-20, Atari ST, Amiga, Mac, Amstrad CPC, and Thomson TO8, updating it for the newer machines in the process. It sold 400,000 copies by 1986, a huge number for the time. It spurred two add-ons, Upper Reaches of Apshai and Curse of Ra, and a prequel, Gateway to Apshai. The first game and its two add-ons were later re-released as the Temple of Apshai trilogy. Epyx released additional games using the same engine, including Crush, Crumble and Chomp!, Rescue at Rigel, and Star Warrior.

A power struggle led Jon Freeman, one of the cofounders, to leave to form Free Fall Associates, who published several hits with Electronic Arts. The remaining cofounder, Jim Connelley took on venture capital and clashed with the new management, leading to his departure as well.
Shifting to arcade-style games

An independent submission from Randy Glover called Jumpman, a platform game with 30 levels inspired by Donkey Kong, changed the company. It became a huge hit on the Commodore 64 and Atari 800, and was ported to the Apple II, IBM PC, and Coleco Vision as well. Epyx shifted focus from strategy/role-playing games to more arcade-like games after the success of Jumpman. This worked, leading to hits like Impossible Mission and Summer Games, a sports game based on the Summer Olympics. Summer Games turned into a series that included Summer Games II, Winter Games, World Games, California Games, The Games: Summer Edition, and The Games: Winter Edition. Epyx’s racing games, Pitstop and Pitstop II, and its Street Sports series, also became classics.
In 1983, Epyx sold $10 million worth of software. That made it the 16th largest software publisher for microcomputers.

The Epyx Fast Load cartridge was a must-have for C-64 owners. By replacing the protocol the C-64 and 1541 used to communicate, it made the 1541 disk drive five times faster. And in case you’re wondering, it worked with other publishers’ games too, not just Epyx titles.
Epyx’s pivot and bankruptcy

But by 1986, Epyx was struggling. It tried to pivot, even creating a game system that became the Atari Lynx. But cashflow problems continued, leading to bankruptcy on October 19, 1989. Epyx’s library didn’t lend itself well to porting to late 80s PCs, partly due to its games’ heavy reliance on sprites. This meant Epyx couldn’t quickly cash in on the popularity of PC gaming like some of its competitors did.

Epyx reorganized but was a shadow of its former self, shrinking from 145 employees to fewer than 20. By 1993, with only 8 employees left, Epyx sold its remaining assets. Bridgestone Media Group bought Epyx’s software library and still owns the rights today.

Bridgestone licensed new versions of many Epyx titles for newer platforms. It also licensed them to be included in retro products like Retro Games’ TheC64 Mini. Of the 65 titles included on TheC64, 20 of them are Epyx titles.

He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.
